Links: [{"title":"gleb kazantsev","url":"https://es.linkedin.com/in/gleb-kazantsev"},{"title":"nicole retter","url":"https://nz.linkedin.com/in/nicole-retter"},{"title":"can a fractional cto rescue a vibe coded mvp","url":"https://solguruz.com/qanda/tech-leadership/can-a-fractional-cto-rescue-a-vibe-coded-mvp/"},{"title":"fractional cto for non technical founders","url":"https://groovyweb.co/blog/fractional-cto-for-non-technical-founders"},{"title":"FRACTIONAL CTO","url":"https://leanware.co/services/fractional-cto"},{"title":"The possibilities are vibe coded","url":"https://mercury.com/blog/vibe-coding-startups-no-code"},{"title":"Hire a Fractional CTO, Eastern Europe | Save up to 70%","url":"https://vamasters.com/fractional-cto-services/"},{"title":"outsourced cto","url":"https://metacto.com/product/outsourced-cto"},{"title":"All articles","url":"https://atarim.io/?p=453"}]

Search results point to a consistent picture: a fractional CTO is commonly pitched as the fix for a non-technical founder whose vibe-coded app has traction but is getting shaky. Most of the sources are vendor marketing, so treat the specifics as their claims.

- **The core pitch:** One source describes the typical case as an app that gains users but hits scaling problems, creating a need for a technical partner. Plenty of non-technical founders are vibe-coding products that actually get traction. But at some point they hit scaling problems and realize they need a technical partner.
- **What the role does:** A SolGuruz piece says the role audits the codebase and decides what to keep, fix, or rebuild (they audit what you've built, decide what to keep, fix, or rebuild, and lead the work). Another source says the job is mostly judgment rather than coding, with the person more than write code, in fact often none at all. Their job is judgment and leadership.
- **Cost:** A Groovyweb guide puts pricing at $8,000 to $25,000 a month depending on stage. That's a single vendor's estimate, so check it against other quotes.
- **Risk of skipping this role:** Mercury-style and Atarim guides warn that fast AI-built apps can accumulate debt and security issues. Atarim notes that tools like Lovable and Bolt allow you to generate technical debt, security flaws, and usability nightmares just as quickly.
- **Alternatives:** Founders often weigh this against hiring developers directly, using an agency, or giving up equity for a cofounder. One article frames the fractional route as avoiding giving up huge chunks of equity for technical help when they've already built a working product.

Overall, the consensus is that a fractional CTO is most useful once a vibe-coded MVP has real users and needs a technical audit, security review, and a keep-fix-or-rebuild decision. Sources disagree on whether it's a long-term fit or a stopgap until a full-time hire.

The exact Reddit thread didn't come up. The results are mostly vendor and agency guides, plus a few Reddit posts from mirror sites, so treat the figures below as secondhand.

**What Reddit discussion surfaced:**
- A r/lovable post argues that Lovable's backend claims are overstated, and asks whether it can handle a large, sudden user load. Although Lovable advertises that it covers back end development, many people seem to claim otherwise.
- Another user reports that a SaaS with multiple API calls and a secure backend took about 300 messages, far more than the 100 they expected. When you want to call multiple APIs, have a solid AND secure backend AND don't know how to code, you need more then that. In my case, i needed around 300 messages to get here.

**What the guides say about when you need a developer:**
- Lovable handles the first stretch well, but the harder part is later. Building a SaaS app with Lovable is genuinely possible, and faster than most people expect for the first 70% of the build. The remaining 30% is where the platform's limits surface: complex billing logic, custom auth rules, edge cases, and production-grade performance.
- Most builds use Supabase underneath, and payment webhook handling and edge cases typically need developer attention.
- Before charging customers, one guide recommends budgeting a few hundred dollars for a developer security review, especially of your database access rules.
- For hiring, one guide suggests filtering for React, TypeScript, and Supabase experience, since that's the stack Lovable generates. It also notes that agencies experienced with taking over and finishing Lovable-built apps ramp up faster.
- Cost estimates vary. One vendor guide puts freelance MVP work at $50-$150/hour or a fixed project bid of $5,000-$15,000, and this is a sales-oriented source, so weigh it accordingly.

Another non-developer launched an iOS app on the App Store and said they hadn't yet validated whether parents would pay for the subscription.
- **Security as the sticking point:** The clearest cautionary tale is a non-technical founder who vibe coded his app without understanding its underlying mechanics, leaving him unaware of its vulnerabilities. He later shut down his app, saying Cursor kept breaking other parts of the code. Commenters suggested offloading payments to an external storefront so the app never stores sensitive customer data.
- **Commenters' view on skills:** Several experienced developers argued that it's not easy for solo founders without real development experience to vibe code a ready-to-go app that wouldn't break in production. Others said the founders who struggle are often the ones who lose sight of the problem they set out to solve once they get caught up in building features.
- **Hiring offers exist:** An agency posted a no-equity offer aimed at non-technical founders, with fixed-price or milestone-based contracts. A non-technical founder also asked for a technical co-founder to maintain the app and help build it out.

I didn't find a thread that directly matches a founder with paying users who is stuck and deciding whether to hire a developer. If you need that exact case, a narrower search such as "paying users" plus "hired a developer" or "rewrite" on Indie Hackers may surface it.
